abstract: Radiologists interpret computed tomography (CT) scans by jointly determining what a finding represents and where it lies in three-dimensional (3D) anatomy. However, deep learning models for CT have largely treated CT interpretation and 3D segmentation as separate tasks, leaving textual findings spatially unverifiable and overlooking potential synergy between clinical understanding and spatial perception. Here we present HoloCT, a generalist 3D foundation model unifying CT interpretation and voxel-level segmentation by jointly modelling whole-volume context and fine-grained anatomical detail, performing diverse clinical tasks while providing 3D masks as evidence. To develop and evaluate HoloCT at scale, we curated HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans from 73 public datasets and six clinical cohorts, with 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT–mask pairs. Across 346 tasks spanning segmentation, lesion screening, visual question answering, and report generation on 61 internal and 12 external datasets, HoloCT outperformed both specialist and foundation models. In multicentre validation across 11,455 clinical CT scans from five hospitals, HoloCT outperformed competing models in lesion segmentation and report generation by 18.2 and 15.3 points. It also achieved 85.1% mean accuracy in screening thyroid tumours and colon lesions, exceeding all four participating radiologists in a retrospective reader study. Further analyses revealed bidirectional semantic–spatial synergy: language-guided segmentation delineated unseen anatomical structures and lesions as well as diffuse free-text findings, outperforming the leading approach by 22.1 points, whereas prompting the model to generate corresponding 3D masks alongside its textual outputs significantly improved interpretation performance. In summary, HoloCT shows that clinical understanding and spatial perception can be learned together within a single foundation model and offers a path towards more accurate and reliable CT analysis.

sections.body: Radiologists link what a finding represents to where it lies in 3D anatomy. Existing systems split these abilities. Segmentation networks localize structures without interpreting them, and CT vision–language models generate text without voxel-level localization. Grounded models connect language and segmentation mainly at the output level, and many use 2D slice encoders or coarsely downsampled 3D inputs. The authors introduce HoloCT, which pairs whole-volume and fine-grained encoders with a language model and a mask decoder. They curate HoloDATA, comprising 195,921 CT scans, 6.2 million instruction dialogues and 2.8 million CT–mask pairs. The introduction states that whether the two abilities can be learned jointly and reinforce each other remains an open question.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing CT models separate report text from 3D segmentation, so findings are hard to verify spatially.

sections.body: HoloCT was evaluated on 346 tasks in 11 formulations, using 61 internal and 12 external public datasets and six clinical cohorts. A single pretrained model was tested without task-specific fine-tuning on internal benchmarks and in zero-shot external and clinical settings. Baselines included nnU-Net, VISTA3D, SAT-Pro, VoxTell, Qwen3-VL-32B, MedGemma 1.5-4B, RadFM-14B, HuluMed-32B and M3D-Phi3-4B. On internal segmentation across 272 categories, HoloCT-8B reached a mean Dice of 0.816, against 0.799 for 82 nnU-Net models. In multi-target screening, macro scores rose from 0.368 to 0.718 internally. HoloCT was also compared with four radiologists in a blinded reader study.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: A single HoloCT model outperforms specialist and foundation models across 346 tasks, including clinical cohorts.

sections.body: The discussion argues that clinical understanding and 3D spatial perception reinforce each other. During training, text-only dialogues improved segmentation accuracy, and mask-paired dialogues improved lesion screening, visual question answering and report generation. At inference, language-guided segmentation generalized zero-shot to unseen anatomy and lesions, and generating 3D masks alongside text improved interpretation without compromising mask quality. The authors note that explicit grounding gave larger gains for HoloCT-4B than for HoloCT-8B. Stated limitations include grounded report generation concentrated in thoracic and abdominal CT, limited accuracy on musculoskeletal bone lesions and diffuse chest findings, single-volume interpretation without prior scans, and a retrospective, single-country hospital evaluation.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Mask-paired training and grounded outputs improve interpretation, but evaluation is retrospective and single-country.

sections.body: HoloCT encodes each CT scan with two branches. A global encoder covers the whole volume, and a detailed encoder keeps fine anatomical detail at 1.5 mm isotropic spacing. The global encoder is Med3DVLM-derived and the detailed encoder is VISTA3D-derived. Projectors produce 256 whole-volume tokens and a grid of fine-grained tokens, one per 32×32×32 voxels, which are passed to a Qwen3-VL language backbone. Segmentation tokens drive a mask decoder with skip connections from the detailed encoder. Training has three stages: vision–language alignment, multitask pre-training and high-quality multitask tuning. Confidence intervals use 1,000 percentile bootstrap resamples of CT scans, and paired comparisons use permutation tests with 10,000 permutations.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: HoloCT couples dual-scale visual encoders with a multimodal language model and mask decoder, trained in three stages.
